teile.einleitung: A scooter is a ride-on toy with a footboard, two or three small wheels and a handlebar. You stand on it with one foot and push off the ground with the other. In Switzerland it is called a “Trottinett”, from the French word “trottinette”; in Germany people say “Tretroller” or “Roller”.
wichtigste: You move an ordinary scooter forward by pushing off with your foot.
The folding scooter with small wheels was invented by the Swiss Wim Ouboter.
An e-scooter has an electric motor and a rechargeable battery.
In Switzerland an e-scooter may go no faster than 20 km/h.
On an e-scooter you must ride on the cycle lane or the road, not on the pavement.
A helmet protects your head when you ride a scooter.

abschnitte.text: A scooter consists of a **footboard**, two or three wheels and a handlebar. You usually brake with your foot on a metal guard over the back wheel or with a hand brake. Many scooters can be folded up and are easy to carry. For small children there are models with three wheels that do not tip over so easily.

Simple wooden scooters existed as children's toys more than a hundred years ago. At the end of the 1990s, the Swiss **Wim Ouboter** in Küsnacht on Lake Zurich developed a light folding aluminium scooter with small wheels. He wanted to cover short distances faster. His company **Micro** made the scooter popular again all over the world.

An **e-scooter** has an electric motor and a rechargeable battery, so you no longer have to push off. In Switzerland it counts as a light moped and may go no faster than **20 km/h**. From 14 to 16 you need a category M driving licence for it; from 16 you no longer do. In many towns you can hire e-scooters using an app.

On an ordinary scooter you count as a pedestrian and may ride on the pavement, but you must be considerate towards others. E-scooters, on the other hand, belong on the **cycle lane** or the road. A **helmet** and lights at dusk make you safer. Only one person should ever stand on a scooter.

With **stunt scooters**, teenagers do jumps and tricks in skateparks. These scooters are built especially sturdily and cannot be folded. There are even competitions in which the best riders show off somersaults and spins. For children the scooter is also a popular way to get to school.

begriffe.erklaerung: The board you stand on when riding a scooter.
A scooter with an electric motor and a rechargeable battery.
A battery that can be charged again.
An especially sturdy scooter for tricks in a skatepark.

gewusst: Wim Ouboter invented his scooter because the way to his favourite sausage stand was too far to walk and too short to drive.
The word “trottinette” comes from the French “trottiner”, which means something like to trot along with little steps.

teile.einleitung: Swiss, whose full name is Swiss International Air Lines, is the largest airline in Switzerland. Its aeroplanes have a red Swiss cross on the tail and fly from Zurich and Geneva to many countries around the world. Swiss was founded in 2002 after the end of the famous Swissair.
wichtigste: There is a Swiss cross on the tail of Swiss aeroplanes.
Swiss was founded in 2002 after Swissair had to ground its planes in 2001.
The most important airport for Swiss is Zurich Airport.
Since 2007, Swiss has belonged to the German Lufthansa Group.
Swiss is a member of the Star Alliance, a group of airlines.
Swiss flies to destinations in Europe, America, Africa and Asia.

abschnitte.text: Swiss is Switzerland's **national airline**. Every year it carries many millions of passengers and also cargo. Its registered office is in Basel, and its most important **hub** is Zurich Airport. From there, large long-haul aircraft fly to places such as New York, Tokyo or Johannesburg.

Swissair, founded in 1931, was the well-known Swiss airline for about 70 years. In October 2001 it ran out of money and all its aircraft had to stay on the ground; this event is called the **grounding**. For many people in Switzerland it was a shock. The regional airline **Crossair** then became the new Swiss in 2002.

In 2005 the German airline **Lufthansa** bought Swiss, and since 2007 it has belonged entirely to the Lufthansa Group. However, Swiss still flies under its own name with the Swiss cross. It is a member of the **Star Alliance**, so travellers can easily change to flights of other partner airlines. The holiday airline Edelweiss also belongs to the same group.

Swiss flies Airbus and Boeing aircraft. For short routes it uses, among others, the **Airbus A220**, which it was one of the first airlines in the world to use. Large aircraft such as the Boeing 777 fly the long routes. The aircraft are looked after by pilots, cabin crew and engineers.

On flights, passengers often get a small piece of **Swiss chocolate**. Announcements are usually made in German, French and English. The red tail with the white cross is a well-known symbol at airports all over the world. Many aircraft are named after Swiss cantons or places.

begriffe.erklaerung: When an airline has to keep all its aircraft on the ground.
A large airport where many of an airline's flights start and passengers change planes.
A group of many airlines that work closely together.
All the aircraft of an airline together.

gewusst: Swiss was one of the first airlines in the world to use the Airbus A220, which was then still called the Bombardier CSeries.
With Swissair, Switzerland lost a company in 2001 that was seen as the country's flying calling card.

teile.einleitung: A tram is an electric railway that runs on rails right through the streets of a town. In Germany it is called “Strassenbahn”; in Switzerland simply “Tram”. Trams carry lots of people through the city quietly and without exhaust fumes.
wichtigste: A tram gets its electricity from an overhead line.
Trams run on rails that are usually set into the road.
Zurich has the largest tram network in Switzerland.
Basel, Bern and Geneva also have tram networks.
The first trams were pulled by horses.
In 1881 the world's first electric tram ran in Berlin.
Basel trams run as far as Germany and France.

abschnitte.text: Above the tracks hangs an **overhead line**, a wire carrying electric current. On the roof of the tram, a **current collector**, also called a bow or pantograph, presses against this wire. The current drives electric motors that turn the wheels. The current flows back through the rails.

The first trams were pulled by **horses**; in Switzerland from 1862 in Geneva. In 1881 the world's first electric tram ran in Berlin-Lichterfelde, built by the company of **Werner von Siemens**. Around 1900 many Swiss towns got electric trams. Later, some towns replaced their trams with buses, but today many towns are building new tram lines again.

**Zurich** has the largest tram network in Switzerland, with many blue trams. Basel has green trams whose lines reach as far as Weil am Rhein in Germany and Saint-Louis in France. Bern and Geneva also have tram networks. New lines include, for example, the Glattalbahn near Zurich and the **Limmattalbahn**, which opened as far as Killwangen in 2022.

A long tram can carry more than 200 people at once. It runs quietly and produces no **exhaust fumes** in the city. Because it runs on its own tracks, it gets stuck in traffic less often than a car. Modern **low-floor trams** have no steps, so people in wheelchairs or with pushchairs can get on easily.

A tram has a much longer **braking distance** than a car and cannot swerve. That is why in Switzerland it usually has right of way. When crossing tram tracks, you should always look carefully both ways. Cyclists should cross the rails as close to a right angle as possible so that the wheel does not get stuck in the groove.

begriffe.erklaerung: A wire carrying electric current above the tracks.
A bow on the roof that takes the current from the overhead line.
A tram with a low floor and no steps at the entrance.
The distance a vehicle needs before it comes to a stop.

gewusst: If a bus leaves every 12 minutes and a tram every 18 minutes, and both start at 8.00, they leave at the same time again at 8.36.
Zurich's Cobra tram was developed and built in Switzerland.

teile.einleitung: The internet is a huge network that connects computers, mobile phones and other devices all over the world. Through the internet we send messages, watch videos, look for information and play together. It has changed our lives as much as printing once did.
wichtigste: The internet connects computers all over the world.
It grew out of ARPANET, which went into operation in the USA in 1969.
Tim Berners-Lee invented the World Wide Web at CERN near Geneva.
Swiss websites often end in “.ch”, which stands for Confoederatio Helvetica.
You never share personal data such as your address and phone number with strangers.
You may only put photos of other people on the internet with their permission.
If something on the internet frightens you, tell an adult you trust.

abschnitte.text: The internet is a network of many millions of computers and networks connected by cables, radio and satellites. So that all devices understand each other, they use shared rules called **protocols**. Data are split into small packets, sent off and put back together at their destination. Every device on the network has its own number, the **IP address**.

The internet grew out of **ARPANET**, a research network in the USA that connected the first computers in 1969. In the 1980s it grew into a worldwide network of universities. From 1989, Tim Berners-Lee developed the World Wide Web with its linked web pages at CERN near Geneva. After that, from the 1990s, the internet also became popular in homes.

The country ending **.ch** stands for Confoederatio Helvetica, the Latin name of Switzerland. Geneva is home to the International Telecommunication Union ITU, which sets worldwide rules for telecommunications and the internet. Some cantons are also trying out **e-voting**, that is, casting your vote electronically over the internet. Comparison websites also help you compare the prices of different suppliers before buying something.

Never share your address, phone number or passwords with strangers. You may only put photos of other people on the internet if they agree. If you see something that frightens you, tell an adult you trust. Before buying online, check the seller and the reviews so that you do not fall for a **scam**.

The internet makes knowledge available to a great many people, much as printing once did. In some countries, however, there is **censorship**, which means the state controls or bans what may appear on the internet. In Switzerland, freedom of opinion and of the media is protected by the Federal Constitution. Even so, the same applies on the internet: insulting others and telling lies about them is forbidden.

begriffe.erklaerung: A fixed rule for how computers exchange data with each other.
A number by which every device on the internet is recognised.
When the state controls or bans what may be published.
Voting in a ballot or election over the internet.

gewusst: Under the oceans lie hundreds of thick undersea cables that carry almost all data traffic between the continents.
The internet and the World Wide Web are not the same thing, because the Web is only one service on the internet, like e-mail.
Today about two thirds of all people in the world use the internet (as of 2024).

teile.einleitung: A tractor is a powerful vehicle used mainly in farming. It pulls ploughs, trailers and many other machines across fields and meadows. In Switzerland people say “Traktor”; in Germany it is often called “Schlepper” or “Trecker”.
wichtigste: A tractor is used mainly in farming.
Tractors have large rear wheels with deep tread so that they do not spin on soft ground.
Many different machines can be attached to a tractor.
Using the power take-off, the tractor can also drive machines.
In Switzerland you may drive a tractor from the age of 14 with a category G licence.
The first tractors were powered by steam.

abschnitte.text: A tractor is a **towing vehicle**, a vehicle built mainly to pull and push. It is not fast, but it is very strong. The large rear wheels with deep **tread** grip the ground well. Many tractors today have four-wheel drive.

At the back and front, a tractor has **hydraulics** that can raise and lower machines such as a plough, harrow or mower. Using the **power take-off**, a turning shaft at the back, the tractor drives, for example, a hay baler or a loader wagon. With a front loader it can lift soil or manure like a small digger. In this way one tractor replaces many working animals and people.

In the past, horses and oxen pulled the plough. In the 19th century there were the first heavy **steam tractors**. Around 1890 the first tractors with petrol engines appeared in the USA. In Switzerland, the company **Hürlimann** in Wil SG built tractors from 1929; Bührer and Vevey were also well-known makers.

There are many tractors on Swiss farms because even steep meadows are farmed. For very steep ground there are special vehicles with a low centre of gravity, called **transporters**, and two-axle mowers. Young people may drive farm vehicles up to 30 km/h from the age of **14** with a category G licence. To get it, they attend a course and take a test.

Today's tractors have comfortable cabs with screens and air conditioning. With the help of **GPS**, they can drive exactly straight across a field almost by themselves. Large tractors have several hundred horsepower. Tractors powered by electricity or biogas are also being developed.

begriffe.erklaerung: A turning shaft on a tractor that drives attached machines.
A technology that lifts heavy things using oil under pressure.
A tool that breaks up the soil and turns it over.
A driving licence for farm vehicles from the age of 14.

gewusst: Some large tractor tyres are taller than an adult.
In tractor pulling competitions, modified tractors pull heavy sledges as far as they can.

teile.einleitung: A computer is a machine that processes data with the help of programs. It can calculate, write, show pictures, play music and much more. Today computers are found not only in laptops but also in smartphones, cars and washing machines.
wichtigste: A computer processes data according to the commands of a program.
Inside, a computer calculates only with the two digits 0 and 1.
In 1941 Konrad Zuse built the first working programmable computer.
The first computers were as big as a room.
Today there is also a small computer inside a smartphone.
The Swiss Niklaus Wirth developed the programming language Pascal at ETH Zurich.
To keep your computer safe, you should never tell anyone your password.

abschnitte.text: The word computer comes from the English “to compute”, which means to calculate. A computer works on the principle of **input, processing, output**. You enter something, the computer processes it and shows a result. The commands telling it what to do are in a **program**. Without programs, a computer would just be a box of metal and plastic.

Inside, a computer calculates only with the two digits 0 and 1, the so-called **binary system**. You can imagine it like a light switch that is either off or on. A single 0 or 1 is called a **bit**; eight bits together make a byte. With many millions of such switches, a computer can represent numbers, letters, pictures and sounds.

The computer's brain is the **processor**; it carries out the commands. The working memory holds data that are needed right now. Files are stored permanently on the hard disk or an SSD. You type letters with the **keyboard**, and you move the pointer on the screen with the mouse. The well-known Swiss company Logitech, founded in the canton of Vaud, makes such mice and keyboards.

In 1941 the German engineer **Konrad Zuse** built the Z3 in Berlin, the first working programmable computer. The first computers were as big as a room and weighed several tonnes. A later machine by Zuse, the Z4, was used at ETH Zurich from 1950. Thanks to small electronic components, transistors and microchips, computers became smaller and faster. From the 1980s, home computers moved into many living rooms.

The Swiss computer scientist **Niklaus Wirth** developed the programming language **Pascal** at ETH Zurich around 1970. Many people all over the world learned to program with it. For his work, Wirth received the Turing Award in 1984, a kind of Nobel Prize for computer science. Not far away, at CERN near Geneva, the World Wide Web was invented in 1989.

In 1997 the computer **Deep Blue** beat the world chess champion Garry Kasparov in a match. In March 2016 the program AlphaGo by DeepMind won 4 to 1 against the Go professional Lee Sedol. Programs like these show what **artificial intelligence** can do. Safety is also important, though: you should never tell anyone your password. You should also only install programs from safe sources.

begriffe.erklaerung: The part of a computer that carries out commands and calculates.
A list of commands that tells the computer what to do.
The smallest unit of information, a 0 or a 1.
A number system that works only with the digits 0 and 1.
A secret word that protects a computer or an account.

gewusst: A smartphone today is much more powerful than the computers used to fly the first people to the Moon in 1969.
The American computer ENIAC from 1946 weighed about 27 tonnes.
The word “bug” for a computer fault became famous when a real moth was found in a computer in 1947.

teile.einleitung: A 3D printer is a machine that makes real objects you can hold. It builds them up layer by layer out of plastic, metal or other materials. In this way it makes toy figures, spare parts and even parts for medicine.
wichtigste: A 3D printer builds objects up layer by layer.
As a template, it needs a three-dimensional computer model.
In home 3D printers, the plastic is fed in as a thread from a reel.
A nozzle melts the plastic thread and lays it down in thin lines.
The first 3D printers were developed in the 1980s.
Experts call the process additive manufacturing.
3D printers are used in industry, medicine, schools and at home.

abschnitte.text: An ordinary printer puts ink onto a flat sheet of paper. A 3D printer, on the other hand, creates objects with length, width and height. It only adds material where it is needed. That is why it is called **additive manufacturing**, because additive means adding. When milling or carving, by contrast, material is taken away.

It starts with a **3D model**, which you draw on a computer or create with a 3D scanner. A special program, the **slicer**, cuts the model into many thin slices. For each slice it works out the exact path of the nozzle. The computer then sends these commands to the printer.

Most home printers use **fused deposition modelling**. A plastic thread, the **filament**, is unwound from a reel and heated to about 200 degrees in a hot nozzle. The nozzle moves back and forth and lays the soft plastic down in fine lines, which quickly harden again. When one layer is finished, it carries on one step higher. With layers of 0.2 millimetres, an object 3 centimetres tall therefore needs 150 layers.

There are also 3D printers that work with liquid resin. A beam of light hardens the resin layer by layer; this is called **stereolithography**. The American Chuck Hull patented this method in the 1980s. Other machines melt fine metal powder together with a **laser**; this is how parts for aircraft are made, for example.

In medicine, made-to-measure **prostheses**, dental splints and models of organs for planning operations are printed. Companies use them to build samples of new products quickly, called prototypes. If you have a broken plastic part, you can sometimes print a spare part yourself. In several countries, small houses have even been built with giant concrete printers.

Many Swiss schools, libraries and so-called makerspaces have their own 3D printers. There, children and teenagers can design and print their own ideas. Universities such as **ETH Zurich** also research new printing methods, for example for concrete buildings. In this way you learn technology, maths and design at the same time.

begriffe.erklaerung: A plastic thread on a reel that a home 3D printer prints with.
A computer program that splits a 3D model into many thin layers.
Making things by adding material layer by layer.
The first sample of a new product, made for testing.

gewusst: A 3D printer has already been tested on the International Space Station ISS so that astronauts can make tools themselves.
A larger object can take many hours or even days in a 3D printer.
A commonly used plastic is PLA, which is made from plants such as maize.

teile.einleitung: A bicycle is a vehicle with two wheels that you power with your muscles. In Germany it is called “Fahrrad”; in Switzerland “Velo”. It is quiet, healthy, environmentally friendly and one of the most important means of transport in the world.
wichtigste: You power a bicycle with your muscles.
The chain connects the pedals to the back wheel.
Karl Drais's running machine from 1817 did not yet have pedals.
A dynamo turns the movement of the wheel into electricity for the lights.
Friction slowly brings a rolling bicycle to a stop.
In Switzerland many children take a cycling test at school.
The tread on the tyre helps it grip better.

abschnitte.text: A bicycle has a **frame**, two wheels with tyres, handlebars, a saddle and pedals. When you push the pedals, the chainring at the front turns, and the **chain** passes the force on to the back wheel. With the **gears** you can ride uphill more easily or go faster on the flat. A little oil on the chain reduces friction.

In 1817, **Karl Drais** in Mannheim invented the running machine, also called the draisine. It did not yet have pedals; you pushed yourself along with your feet. Later came the **penny-farthing** with its huge front wheel and, around 1885, the safety bicycle with chain drive, which looks like our bicycles today. In 1888, John Boyd Dunlop's air-filled tyre made riding much more comfortable.

In Switzerland a roadworthy bicycle needs two brakes, a bell, lights at the front and back, and reflectors. A **dynamo** turns the movement of the wheel into electricity for the lights; today there are also battery lights. When you stop pedalling, **friction** and air resistance slowly bring the bicycle to a stop. If you ride at 15 kilometres per hour, you travel 30 kilometres in two hours.

In Switzerland there are thousands of kilometres of **cycle paths** and signposted cycle routes from “Veloland Schweiz”. Children up to 12 may ride on the pavement if there is no cycle lane, and they must be considerate towards pedestrians. Many schools have a **cycling test**. A cycle helmet is not compulsory but is strongly recommended.

Cycle races such as the **Tour de France** or the Tour de Suisse, which has existed since 1933, are very popular. There are racing bikes, mountain bikes, BMX bikes and **e-bikes** with electric motors. When you cycle, you get exercise and produce no exhaust fumes. That is why the bicycle is good for your health and for the environment.

begriffe.erklaerung: The first two-wheeler, by Karl Drais, without pedals.
A small generator that makes electricity from movement.
A device that lets you pedal more easily or with more effort.
A force that slows down a movement.

gewusst: It is estimated that there are more than twice as many bicycles as cars in the world.
On a penny-farthing the front wheel was often more than 1.5 metres tall, so that each turn of the pedals took you a long way.

teile.einleitung: A ship is a large watercraft that carries people and goods across seas, lakes and rivers. People were already building ships out of wood thousands of years ago; today the largest are made of steel and are longer than three football pitches. Even though they are so heavy, they do not sink.
wichtigste: A steel ship floats because it pushes aside a lot of water and buoyancy holds it up.
Large cargo ships travel up the Rhine as far as Basel.
In the past, the wind drove the explorers' ships.
Columbus set off in 1492 with three ships; the largest was the Santa María.
From 1519 to 1522, Magellan's expedition was the first to sail all the way around the world.
Today, container ships carry most of the world's goods.
Switzerland also has ocean-going ships; their home port is Basel.

abschnitte.text: A ship's hull pushes water aside; we say it **displaces** water. The water pushes back from below, and this force is called **buoyancy**. If the displaced water weighs as much as the whole ship, the ship floats. The Greek scholar Archimedes discovered this more than 2000 years ago.

The front part is called the **bow**, the back part the **stern**. Looking forward, the left side is **port** and the right side is starboard. The rudder is used for steering, and a propeller under the water drives modern ships. The ship is steered from the bridge, where the captain is in command.

For a long time, the **wind** drove ships across the seas. In 1492, Christopher **Columbus** set off with three ships, the Santa María, the Pinta and the Niña, and first stopped in the Canary Islands. He then crossed the Atlantic and reached America. From 1519 to 1522, Ferdinand **Magellan**'s expedition was the first to sail all the way around the Earth.

There are **container ships**, tankers for crude oil, ferries for cars, cruise ships for holidays and fishing boats. The largest container ships are about 400 metres long and carry more than 20,000 containers. Icebreakers can break through thick ice. Warships and submarines belong to a country's navy.

Although Switzerland has no coast, large cargo ships travel up the **Rhine** as far as **Basel**. In the Rhine ports, containers, grain and fuel are unloaded and reloaded. Since 1941 there has been a Swiss ocean-going fleet whose ships are registered in Basel. Many passenger boats also take people on trips on the Swiss lakes.

begriffe.erklaerung: The force of water that pushes floating things upwards.
The front part of a ship.
The back part of a ship.
The left side of a ship when you look forward.
A large metal box of standard size for goods.

gewusst: Because they can travel through the desert for weeks, camels are also called “ships of the desert”.
In 1912 the Titanic was thought to be unsinkable, yet it sank on its first voyage after hitting an iceberg.

teile.einleitung: A sailing ship is a ship driven by the wind. The wind blows into large pieces of cloth, the sails, and pushes the ship forward. For centuries, sailing ships were the fastest way to travel across the seas.
wichtigste: A sailing ship is driven by the wind.
The sails hang from masts and are adjusted with ropes.
Many explorers used caravels.
With clever technique, a sailing ship can even travel at an angle against the wind.
The Swiss team Alinghi won the America's Cup in 2003.
Today most people sail in their free time or as a sport.

abschnitte.text: A sailing ship has a **hull**, one or more **masts** and sails made of cloth. All the ropes and masts together are called the **rigging**. Under the hull, a keel stops the ship drifting sideways or capsizing. It is steered with the rudder at the stern.

If the wind comes from behind, the ship is simply pushed along. If it blows from the side, the sail works like a wing and pulls the ship forward. No sailing ship can sail directly into the wind. That is why it sails in a zigzag; this is called **tacking**.

In the 15th and 16th centuries, Portuguese and Spanish seafarers used **caravels**. These nimble ships could sail well even when the wind was unfavourable. In 1492, Christopher Columbus sailed to America with two caravels and one larger ship. Later the Dutch and the English built large merchant ships for the route to Asia.

In the 19th century the fast **clippers**, which brought tea from China to Europe, were famous. The “Cutty Sark” from 1869 can still be seen in London today. Huge cargo sailing ships were called windjammers. When steamships came along, the great sailing ships gradually disappeared.

People sail on many Swiss lakes, especially Lake Geneva, Lake Constance and Lake Zurich. Every year the **Bol d'Or** regatta takes place on Lake Geneva. The Geneva team **Alinghi**, owned by Ernesto Bertarelli, won the America's Cup in 2003 as the first European team and defended it in 2007. That was a sensation for a country without a sea.

begriffe.erklaerung: All the masts, sails and ropes of a sailing ship together.
Sailing in a zigzag against the wind.
A nimble sailing ship used by explorers in the 15th and 16th centuries.
A race between sailing boats.

gewusst: The America's Cup is one of the oldest sports trophies still contested in the world and dates from 1851.
Today some cargo ships are being fitted with large sails again to save fuel.

teile.einleitung: A steam engine is a machine driven by hot steam. It turns the heat from burning fuel into movement. Without it there would have been no Industrial Revolution with its factories, steam locomotives and steamships.
wichtigste: A steam engine is driven by hot steam.
In 1712 Thomas Newcomen built the first workable steam engine.
The first steam engines mainly pumped water out of mines.
James Watt improved the steam engine decisively and patented it in 1769.
The fuel burned was mainly coal.
The steam engine was the driving force of the Industrial Revolution.
The unit of power, the watt, is named after James Watt.

abschnitte.text: In a **boiler**, water is heated by a fire until it turns into steam. Steam takes up much more space than water and therefore pushes hard against a movable **piston** in a cylinder. The piston moves back and forth. Using a rod and a flywheel, this is turned into a rotating movement that drives wheels, pumps or machines.

In 1712 the Englishman **Thomas Newcomen** built the first steam engine that really worked reliably. It was used mainly in coal and tin mines, where groundwater kept flowing into the tunnels. The engine pumped this water up so that the miners could dig deeper. However, it was huge and slow and used a great deal of coal.

The Scot **James Watt** realised that Newcomen's engine wasted a lot of energy because the cylinder was cooled down again and again. He invented a separate **condenser**, in which the steam is cooled outside the cylinder. In 1769 he patented his improved engine. It needed only about a quarter of the coal and could later also supply rotating movement for factories. To show how strong his engines were, Watt compared them with horses and introduced the unit **horsepower**.

The **Industrial Revolution** is the name for the change to working with machines and factories from the 18th century onwards. Before that, factories needed a water wheel and therefore had to stand beside a river. With the steam engine they could be built anywhere, for example in towns or next to coal pits. Spinning and weaving mills now produced much more cloth in much less time.

At the beginning of the 19th century, steam engines were put on wheels, and so the **steam locomotive** was born. Steamships also now sailed across seas and lakes. The first railway entirely on Swiss soil ran between Zurich and Baden in 1847 and was called the “Spanisch-Brötli-Bahn”. Historic paddle steamers still sail on many Swiss lakes today, for example Lake Lucerne and Lake Geneva.

Today our machines are mostly driven by electric motors and combustion engines. But the principle of steam has not disappeared. In many power stations, steam turbines turn the generators that produce electricity. In honour of James Watt, the unit of power is called the **watt**, which you will find on every light bulb and every hairdryer.

begriffe.erklaerung: A movable part in the cylinder that the steam pushes back and forth.
A container in which steam is cooled and turns back into water.
The period from the 18th century in which machines and factories replaced handwork.
An old unit of power, abbreviated hp.

gewusst: Even in ancient Greece, Hero of Alexandria built a small steam ball that spun round, but only as a toy.
The “Spanisch-Brötli-Bahn” got its name because servants could use it to bring fresh pastries from Baden to Zurich.
The steamships on Lake Geneva are among the largest paddle steamer fleets in the world.

teile.einleitung: A television is a device that receives moving pictures and sounds and shows them on a screen. The word “television” actually means “seeing far away”. Since the 1950s, television has changed the way people experience news, sport and entertainment.
wichtigste: The television shows pictures and sounds that are transmitted from far away.
In 1926 in London, John Logie Baird was one of the first to show moving television pictures.
The first television pictures were black and white.
Switzerland has had regular television since 1953.
A screen picture is made of tiny dots, the pixels.
In 1969 millions of people watched the Moon landing live on television.
Swiss households pay a media fee for radio and television with a public service mission.

abschnitte.text: A television receives broadcasts via aerial, cable, satellite or the internet and turns them into picture and sound. The picture is made up of millions of tiny **pixels** that light up in red, green and blue. Because the pictures are shown very quickly one after another, our eyes see smooth movement. With the **remote control** you can change channels comfortably from the sofa.

Many inventors were working on television at the same time. In 1926 in London, the Scot **John Logie Baird** was one of the first to show moving television pictures. His pictures were small, flickered and were black and white. Later, electronic sets with a **picture tube** took over; for a long time they were heavy and bulky.

In Switzerland regular television broadcasting began in 1953, at first only on a few evenings a week. Today **SRG** broadcasts in all the national languages; in German-speaking Switzerland it is called **SRF**. It is financed mainly by the media fee, which is collected by the company Serafe. Every household pays it, whether or not it owns a set.

On 21 July 1969, millions of people all over the world watched live as Neil Armstrong stepped onto the Moon. Football World Cups and the Olympic Games are also watched on television by billions of people. From the 1960s and 1970s, colour televisions came into living rooms. Today flat screens with **LED** or OLED technology are usual.

**Screen time** is the time you spend in front of a mobile phone, tablet or television. Too much of it can make you tired and leaves less time for exercise, friends and sleep. It helps to agree rules with your parents and to choose programmes on purpose. Many televisions today are connected to the internet as smart TVs and also serve as a screen for games consoles such as the Nintendo Switch.

begriffe.erklaerung: A tiny dot that a screen picture is made of.
A large glass tube that produced the picture in old televisions.
A charge in Switzerland for radio and television with a public service mission.
A television with an internet connection for apps and streaming.

gewusst: A modern 4K picture is made up of more than eight million pixels.
John Logie Baird's first television pictures had only 30 lines.
Old tube televisions were so deep that they looked almost like a box.

teile.einleitung: A glider is an aeroplane without an engine. It glides silently through the air and uses rising air to gain height. Good pilots can fly them for hours and cover hundreds of kilometres.
wichtigste: A glider has no engine.
Warm rising air that glider pilots use is called a thermal.
Gliders have very long, narrow wings.
They are launched with a winch or towed behind a powered aeroplane.
Without rising air, a glider sinks slowly but steadily.
From 1891, Otto Lilienthal made the first successful gliding flights.

abschnitte.text: A glider glides slowly downwards like a paper aeroplane. As it does, air flows over the **wings** and creates lift, which holds it up. To stay up longer, the pilot looks for **updraughts**, that is, air that is rising. There the pilot circles and so gains height again.

When the sun warms the ground, warm air rises in bubbles; this is a **thermal**. Fluffy cumulus clouds often show where a thermal is. When the wind blows against a mountain, the air is pushed upwards; this is called **ridge lift**. In the Alps and the Jura, Swiss glider pilots use both.

Because it has no engine, a glider needs help to take off. In a **winch launch**, a winch pulls it up into the air on a long cable. In an aerotow, a powered aeroplane pulls it up and then the glider releases the rope. It lands at an airfield or, in an emergency, in a field.

Modern gliders are made of light **plastic** reinforced with glass or carbon fibres. Their wings are usually 15 to more than 25 metres long. They are built so that from a height of one kilometre they can glide 40 to more than 60 kilometres. Important instruments are the altimeter and the variometer, which shows climbing and sinking.

From 1891, the German aviation pioneer **Otto Lilienthal** made thousands of gliding flights with wings he built himself. In the 1920s, gliding developed into a sport on the Wasserkuppe mountain in Germany. Today there are competitions and championships all over the world. The longest glider flight covered more than 3000 kilometres.

begriffe.erklaerung: Warm air rising from the ground.
How many metres an aircraft glides forward for every metre of height it loses.
An instrument that shows whether the aircraft is climbing or sinking.
A take-off in which a winch pulls the aircraft up.

gewusst: Birds such as storks and eagles also circle in thermals to gain height without flapping their wings.
Glider pilots can sometimes stay in the air for several hours without using a single drop of fuel.

teile.einleitung: CERN is the largest research centre for particle physics in the world and is located near Geneva. There, experts from many countries work together to find out what everything in the universe is made of. The World Wide Web was also invented at CERN.
wichtigste: CERN is near Geneva, right on the border between Switzerland and France.
It was founded in 1954, and Switzerland was one of the founding countries.
It is home to the world's largest particle accelerator, the Large Hadron Collider.
In 2012 the Higgs particle was detected at CERN.
From 1989, Tim Berners-Lee invented the World Wide Web there.
On 30 April 1993, CERN released the Web for everyone to use freely.
Many countries work together peacefully at CERN.

abschnitte.text: CERN is a research centre where countries study physics together. The name comes from the French “Conseil européen pour la recherche nucléaire”, meaning European Council for Nuclear Research. Scientists there study the smallest building blocks of matter, the **elementary particles**. CERN was founded in 1954 by twelve European states, including Switzerland. Today it has more than 20 member states, and thousands of researchers from all over the world take part.

The headquarters is in **Meyrin** in the canton of Geneva, near the airport. The large facilities reach underground as far as France. CERN is one of the best-known research centres in Switzerland. Visitors can explore the Science Gateway visitor centre, which opened in 2023.

The heart of CERN is the **Large Hadron Collider**, LHC for short. It is a ring-shaped tunnel about 27 kilometres round, lying about 100 metres deep underground. Inside it, tiny particles are accelerated to almost the speed of light and then made to collide. Huge measuring instruments, the **detectors**, record what is produced in the collisions. For the powerful magnets to work, they are cooled to about minus 271 degrees, colder than outer space.

In 2012, researchers at CERN announced that they had detected the **Higgs boson**. This elementary particle helps to explain how other particles get their mass. Physicists such as Peter Higgs had already predicted it in the 1960s. In 2013, Peter Higgs and François Englert received the Nobel Prize in Physics for it.

The British computer scientist **Tim Berners-Lee** worked at CERN and wanted researchers to be able to share their information more easily. From 1989 he developed the **World Wide Web** for this, with web pages, links and the first browser. On 30 April 1993, CERN released the Web for everyone to use freely. Without this decision, the internet would look very different today.

begriffe.erklaerung: Research into the very smallest building blocks of everything.
A machine that makes tiny particles extremely fast.
An elementary particle that explains how other particles get their mass.
A network of web pages connected by links.

gewusst: The particles in the LHC race round the whole 27-kilometre ring more than 11,000 times a second.
Antimatter is also made and studied at CERN.
The very first website in the world ran on a computer at CERN.

teile.einleitung: GPS is a satellite system that lets you find your exact location almost anywhere on Earth. The abbreviation stands for “Global Positioning System”. Whether in the car, on a mobile phone or when hiking, GPS helps us find our way.
wichtigste: GPS helps you find your own location.
The system was developed by the US military.
About 30 satellites circle the Earth at a height of about 20,000 kilometres for it.
A receiver needs signals from at least four satellites.
The satellites carry very accurate atomic clocks on board.
Europe has its own system called Galileo.
Smartphones usually use several systems at once.

abschnitte.text: GPS is a **satellite navigation system** from the USA. The US Department of Defense started it in the 1970s and made it fully usable from 1995. At first it was intended mainly for the military. Today anyone in the world can use it free of charge.

Every GPS satellite constantly sends out a radio signal with the exact time and its position. A receiver measures how long the signals take to reach it and from this calculates its distance from the satellites. With the signals from at least four satellites, it can work out its location and its height. For this to work, the satellites have extremely accurate **atomic clocks** on board.

Besides GPS there are other systems: **Galileo** from Europe, GLONASS from Russia and BeiDou from China. Galileo was built by the European Union and the European Space Agency ESA and has been in operation since 2016. Switzerland takes part in Galileo, and Swiss companies supplied atomic clocks for it, for example. Modern mobile phones receive several of these systems at once and are therefore more accurate.

Thanks to GPS, the **satnav** in the car shows the way and warns of traffic jams. On hikes in the Alps, an app on your phone shows where you are on the map. Aircraft, ships, rescue services and farmers with tractors also use satellite navigation. Even delivery services and cycling apps work with it.

Many apps want to know where you are right now. That can be useful, but it also reveals a lot about you. So it is worth allowing **location access** in the settings only for selected apps. Never share your exact location with strangers on the internet.

begriffe.erklaerung: A spacecraft that circles the Earth in an orbit.
An extremely accurate clock that is hardly a second out in millions of years.
Finding and following the right way.
The European satellite navigation system.

gewusst: If the satellites' clocks were only one millionth of a second wrong, the calculated location would be about 300 metres off.
Because of Albert Einstein's theory of relativity, the clocks in space tick slightly faster than on Earth and have to be adjusted.
The European system is named after the Italian scientist Galileo Galilei.

teile.einleitung: Printing is a process that lets you copy texts quickly and in large numbers. In Europe, Johannes Gutenberg invented printing with movable type around 1450. This invention changed the world, because suddenly many more people could own and read books.
wichtigste: Before printing, books were copied by hand.
In the Middle Ages, monks often copied the books.
Around 1450 in Mainz, Johannes Gutenberg invented printing with movable type.
Movable type means single metal letters that can be put together again and again.
With the printing press, the paper is pressed onto the inked letters.
Gutenberg's printing press was similar to a wine press.
Printing made books cheaper and helped spread knowledge quickly.

abschnitte.text: Before there was printing, books in Europe were mostly copied by hand. This work was often done by **monks** in the writing rooms of monasteries. Copying a single book could take months or even years. That is why books were very expensive and only a few people owned any. A famous example of manuscripts is the Abbey Library at the monastery of St Gallen.

**Johannes Gutenberg** lived from about 1400 to 1468 in Mainz, a town on the Rhine in what is now Germany. He was a goldsmith and knew a lot about metal. Around 1450 he developed a method of printing books with movable letters. His best-known work is the **Gutenberg Bible**, which was finished around 1454.

Gutenberg's most important idea was **movable type**, that is, single letters made of metal. He cast them with a special hand mould so that they were always the same size. The compositor arranged the letters into words, lines and whole pages. After printing, the letters were taken apart again and used for the next page.

The set page was coated with a thick ink. A sheet of paper was laid on top and pressed firmly down with the **printing press**. This press was similar to a wine press, of the kind used to squeeze grapes. In this way many identical pages could be made in a short time.

Books became cheaper, and more and more people learned to read. New ideas from science and religion spread much faster than before. The **Reformation** led by Martin Luther and Huldrych Zwingli would hardly have become known so quickly without printed writings. **Pamphlets** and later newspapers also came about through printing. That is why many experts count printing among the most important inventions of humankind.

Only a few decades after Gutenberg, there were print shops in Swiss towns. **Basel** in particular became an important printing town with many workshops. There, for example, the scholar Erasmus of Rotterdam worked together with the printer Johann Froben. Important print shops were also set up in Zurich and Geneva.

begriffe.erklaerung: A single cast letter used for printing.
A craftsman who arranges the letters into lines and pages.
A machine that presses the paper firmly onto the inked letters.
A book written by hand.

gewusst: As early as around the year 1040, a Chinese man named Bi Sheng printed with movable characters made of clay.
Just under 50 copies of the Gutenberg Bible still exist today; they are among the most valuable books in the world.
The pages of the Gutenberg Bible usually have 42 lines, which is why it is also called the 42-line Bible.

teile.einleitung: A Zeppelin is a huge airship with a rigid frame that is filled with gas. It is named after its inventor, Count Ferdinand von Zeppelin. About a hundred years ago, people even travelled across the Atlantic in Zeppelins.
wichtigste: A Zeppelin floats because it is filled with a gas that is lighter than air.
It was invented by Count Ferdinand von Zeppelin.
The first Zeppelin, LZ 1, took off on Lake Constance in 1900.
Zeppelins have a rigid frame made of light metal.
In 1937 the hydrogen-filled “Hindenburg” burned up in the USA.
Today's Zeppelins are filled with helium, which does not burn.

abschnitte.text: A Zeppelin contains large **gas cells** with a gas that is lighter than air. This gives it **lift**, similar to a hot-air balloon. Propellers with engines drive it forward, and it is steered with rudders at the back. Unlike a balloon, a Zeppelin can therefore fly in a chosen direction.

A typical feature of a Zeppelin is its **rigid frame** of light metal, covered with fabric. That is why it is also called a rigid airship. Underneath hangs the **gondola**, where the crew and passengers sit. Airships without a rigid frame, on the other hand, are called non-rigid airships or blimps.

**Count Ferdinand von Zeppelin** launched his first Zeppelin, the LZ 1, on 2 July 1900 over **Lake Constance** near Friedrichshafen. In the First World War, Zeppelins were also used for attacks. In 1929 the LZ 127 “Graf Zeppelin” flew around the Earth. In the 1930s, Zeppelins carried passengers in comfort to North and South America.

The **“Hindenburg”** was about 245 metres long and one of the largest aircraft ever built. On 6 May 1937 it caught fire while landing in Lakehurst in the USA. Because it was filled with flammable **hydrogen**, it burned out within seconds, and 36 people died. After that, the era of the great passenger Zeppelins came to an end.

Since the 1990s there has been the **Zeppelin NT**, a modern design using helium, which does not burn. It flies tourists over Lake Constance and can easily be seen from the Swiss shore. Zeppelins are also used for advertising, research and filming for television. In Friedrichshafen, a Zeppelin Museum shows the history of airships.

begriffe.erklaerung: An aircraft that floats thanks to a gas lighter than air and has engines.
A very light gas that burns easily.
A light gas that does not burn.
A cabin under an airship or balloon.

gewusst: The Hindenburg was almost as long as three football pitches end to end.
Count Ferdinand von Zeppelin was already over 60 years old when his first airship took off.

teile.einleitung: A bridge is a structure that leads over an obstacle such as a river, a valley or a road. Even in the Stone Age, people laid tree trunks across streams. Today there are bridges made of wood, stone, steel and concrete, and some are many kilometres long.
wichtigste: Bridges carry paths, roads or railway lines over obstacles.
On a suspension bridge, the roadway hangs from strong cables.
The Chapel Bridge in Lucerne is a famous wooden bridge.
A legend involving the Devil surrounds the Devil's Bridge in the Schöllenen Gorge.
Castles had drawbridges that could be pulled up.
The longest bridge in the world is a railway viaduct in China about 165 kilometres long (as of 2026).
Important types of bridge are beam, arch, suspension and cable-stayed bridges.

abschnitte.text: A bridge spans an obstacle so that people, vehicles or trains can get across. The supports it stands on are called **piers**. The distance between two supports is the **span**. A bridge must carry its own weight, the traffic, the wind and sometimes snow. That is why engineers calculate every bridge precisely.

The simplest form is the **beam bridge**, in which a girder lies on supports. An **arch bridge** carries the weight through an arch into the ground; this is how the Romans built bridges and aqueducts of stone. On a **suspension bridge**, the roadway hangs from strong cables stretched over tall towers. A famous example is the Golden Gate Bridge in San Francisco. On cable-stayed bridges, the cables run diagonally straight from the tower to the roadway.

In the Middle Ages, castles protected themselves with a moat and a **drawbridge** that could be pulled up when there was danger. Bridges were important trade routes, so a bridge toll was often charged. In wartime, bridges were often destroyed so that enemies could not cross. With the railway in the 19th century, many new bridges of iron and steel were built.

The **Chapel Bridge** in Lucerne crosses the River Reuss and dates from the 14th century. It is thought to be one of the oldest surviving covered wooden bridges in Europe and is decorated with painted panels. In 1993 a large part of it burned down; afterwards it was rebuilt. Next to it stands the eight-sided Water Tower. Also well known are the Landwasser Viaduct of the Rhaetian Railway near Filisur and the many railway bridges on the Gotthard.

The **Devil's Bridge** in the canton of Uri leads through the wild Schöllenen Gorge on the way to the Gotthard. According to legend, the Devil helped the people of Uri build it and in return demanded the first soul to cross the bridge. The clever people of Uri sent a billy goat across first. Very close by, a monument commemorates the Russian general **Suvorov**, who marched through the Alps with his army in 1799.

The longest bridge in the world is in China; it is a railway viaduct about 165 kilometres long (as of 2026). That is about as far as from Zurich to Bern and some of the way back again. The highest bridge, the Duge Bridge in China, is more than 500 metres above a valley. Such record-breaking structures show how advanced **construction technology** is today.

begriffe.erklaerung: A strong support that a bridge stands on.
The distance between two supports of a bridge.
A long bridge with many arches or piers across a valley.
A bridge at a castle that could be pulled up.

gewusst: The Chapel Bridge is one of the most photographed structures in Switzerland.
There are also bridges that turn or open up so that ships can pass through.
Some bridges are built only for animals, so that wild animals can cross motorways safely.

teile.einleitung: A light bulb, more precisely an incandescent lamp, is a lamp in which a thin wire gets so hot that it shines brightly. For more than a hundred years it lit up homes all over the world. Because it wastes a lot of electricity, it has now been replaced almost everywhere by LED lamps.
wichtigste: In a light bulb, a thin glowing wire gives off light.
A light bulb needs electric current to shine.
From 1879, Thomas Edison made the light bulb practical for everyday use.
The German name “Glühbirne” comes from the fact that the lamp looks like a pear (“Birne”).
A light bulb gets hot when it is on.
It turns most of the electricity into heat instead of light.
That is why it was replaced by more economical LED lamps.

abschnitte.text: When electric current flows through a very thin wire, the **filament**, it gets very hot. At about 2500 degrees Celsius it glows bright white and gives off light. Today the wire is usually made of **tungsten**, a metal that only melts at very high temperatures. So that the wire does not burn up, the glass bulb does not contain normal air but a protective gas or a vacuum.

Even before 1879, various researchers built glowing lamps, for example the Englishman **Joseph Swan**. But their lamps only lasted a short time. From 1879, **Thomas Edison** from the USA made the light bulb practical for everyday use by finding a long-lasting filament made of carbonised fibres. He also built electricity networks and power stations so that the lamps could shine in homes at all.

A classic light bulb turns only about five per cent of the electricity into light. The rest becomes heat, which is why it gets very hot after a short time. The power of a lamp is given in **watts**, named after James Watt. An old 60-watt light bulb is about as bright as an LED lamp of only around 8 watts.

To save energy, the European Union and Switzerland gradually banned the sale of most light bulbs from 2009. They were replaced first by energy-saving lamps and then by **LED** lamps. LEDs last much longer, hardly get warm and need only a fraction of the electricity. The familiar bulb shape still exists, but now with LED technology inside.

A torch needs a battery as its power source so that its little bulb can shine. In the past, torches, bicycle lights and car headlights also had small light bulbs in them. Today you find LEDs almost everywhere. Even so, the light bulb is still a symbol of a good idea, which is why comics often show a glowing bulb above a character who has an idea.

begriffe.erklaerung: The thin wire in a light bulb that shines when it glows.
A metal that does not melt until it is above 3400 degrees.
A light-emitting diode, a very economical electric light source.
The unit that shows how much electricity a device uses per second.

gewusst: In a fire station in Livermore, California, a light bulb has been burning almost without a break since 1901.
Edison and his team tested thousands of materials before they found a good filament.
A light bulb can get so hot that you can burn your fingers on it.

teile.einleitung: A submarine is a ship that can travel under water. The German name “U-Boot” is short for “Unterseeboot”, meaning undersea boat. Submarines can dive, travel long distances under water and surface again.
wichtigste: A submarine travels under water.
To dive, a submarine fills its ballast tanks with water.
To surface, the water is pushed out again with compressed air.
With a periscope you can look above the surface from under water.
In both world wars submarines sank many ships.
In 1960 the Swiss Jacques Piccard reached the bottom of the Mariana Trench.
Captain Nemo's Nautilus from a novel by Jules Verne is famous.

abschnitte.text: A submarine has large **ballast tanks**. When they are filled with air, the boat floats on the surface. When water is let in, it becomes heavier and dives. To surface, **compressed air** pushes the water out again.

Under water it is dark, and most submarines have no windows. Just below the surface, the crew looks through a **periscope**, a tube with mirrors. In the depths, submarines find their way with **sonar**, which sends out sound waves and measures the echo. Dolphins find their way in a similar way.

As early as 1775, the American David Bushnell built a small diving boat called the Turtle. In 1870, **Jules Verne**'s novel “Twenty Thousand Leagues Under the Sea” was published, featuring Captain Nemo's submarine Nautilus. In the First World War, in 1915, a German submarine sank the British passenger ship **Lusitania**, killing many Americans too. From 1 February 1917, Germany waged unrestricted submarine warfare, in which even neutral merchant ships were sunk without warning.

Today many navies have large **nuclear submarines** that can stay under water for months. The first of these was the American USS Nautilus in 1954. Smaller submarines run on diesel and batteries. There are also research submarines and even submarines for tourists.

The Swiss scientist **Auguste Piccard** developed a deep-sea diving vessel, the bathyscaphe. On 23 January 1960, his son **Jacques Piccard** and Don Walsh dived almost 11,000 metres in the bathyscaphe Trieste to the bottom of the **Mariana Trench**. This is the deepest point of all the oceans. For the 1964 Swiss National Exhibition, Jacques Piccard built the tourist submarine “Auguste Piccard”, which took tens of thousands of visitors through Lake Geneva.

begriffe.erklaerung: A tank in a submarine that is filled with water to dive.
A viewing tube used to look above the surface from under water.
Locating things under water using sound waves.
A special diving vessel for very great depths.

gewusst: At the bottom of the Mariana Trench, the water presses more than a thousand times harder than at the surface.
The Nautilus in the novel is named after the nautilus, a relative of the squid with a shell.
